subject: chemistry
question_text: Define the dipole moment. Why is the dipole moment of the BF₃ molecule zero?

verification.note: Chapter 3 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.56-61), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. This is the second of the book's two dipole-moment SAQs (SAQ 9); it shares only the definition with the applications form (SAQ 8), so the two are separate cards, not cuts.

steps.label: Definition
lines: Dipole moment (μ): the product of the
magnitude of the charge on either pole and
the distance between the two poles of a
polar molecule.
It is a vector quantity, so bond moments
add as vectors.
steps.why: The vector sentence is what connects the definition to the BF₃ argument: only vectors can cancel, and cancellation is the whole answer.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the vector line. Without it the cancellation argument in the next steps has no basis.
steps.memory_tip: Charge times distance, and it is a vector — the vector part is what this question uses.
steps.margin_note: End the definition with the vector sentence; the rest of the answer stands on it.

steps.label: Geometry of BF₃
lines: BF₃ is trigonal planar: the three B−F
bonds lie in one plane at 120° to each
other.
Each B−F bond is polar (F is more
electronegative than B), so each bond has
its own bond moment pointing toward F.
steps.why: The zero total is a property of the symmetric arrangement, so the geometry — planar, 120° — must be stated before the cancellation can be argued.
common_mistakes: Calling BF₃ pyramidal. Boron has NO lone pair, so the molecule is flat.
Saying the B−F bonds are non-polar. Each bond IS polar; it is the sum that is zero.
steps.memory_tip: No lone pair on boron, so BF₃ is flat with three equal arrows at 120°.
steps.margin_note: Three polar bonds at 120° — both facts feed the next step.

steps.label: The cancellation
lines: The three bond moments are equal in
magnitude and at 120° to each other.
The resultant of any two of them is equal
in magnitude and opposite in direction to
the third.
So the vector sum of all three is zero.
steps.why: This is the actual mechanism: two moments at 120° add to a resultant that exactly opposes the third, so the three sum to zero.
common_mistakes: Saying the moments are zero. Each moment is non-zero; only their SUM is zero.
Asserting cancellation without the any-two-oppose-the-third sentence, which is the reason.
steps.memory_tip: Any two arrows at 120° add up to the exact opposite of the third.
steps.margin_note: The any-two-against-the-third sentence is the mark here.

steps.label: The conclusion

lines.text: μ(BF₃) = 0 — the three bond moments cancel

lines: Each B−F bond is polar, but the symmetric
trigonal planar shape makes the molecule
as a whole non-polar.
steps.why: The closing sentence resolves the apparent contradiction the question is built on: polar bonds, yet a non-polar molecule, because of symmetry.
common_mistakes: Concluding that BF₃ has non-polar bonds. The bonds stay polar; the molecule is non-polar.
steps.memory_tip: Polar bonds, symmetric shape, zero total.
steps.margin_note: Box the equation with its five-word reason.

insider_note: The reason must be a vector argument — any two bond moments add to the exact opposite of the third. Polar bonds, non-polar molecule is the sentence to write.
